coverage: Substantive reading of PDF pages 793–994, covering nuclear strategy, Korea, Eisenhower institutions, Soviet succession, Iran, Suez, Cuba, and Asian/African decolonization; selected late-book analysis pp 1011,1031–1034 and concluding 1963–1964 developments pp 1088–1090. Summaries exclude recognizable bracketed editorial interpolations. Citations use PDF page numbers, not printed-page labels.

people.name: Lewis L. Strauss
people.role: Investment banker and Atomic Energy Commission chairman
people.description: Quigley connects Strauss’s investment-banking background with his leadership of the AEC and his opposition to Oppenheimer. The book portrays him as a central advocate of secrecy and nuclear strategy associated with the Eisenhower administration.

people.name: J. Robert Oppenheimer
people.description: Quigley emphasizes Oppenheimer’s advocacy of diversified nuclear weapons, tactical defense and air defense, and treats the loss of his security clearance as an institutional struggle over strategy rather than proof of espionage.

people.name: Edward Teller
people.description: Quigley describes Teller’s lobbying for thermonuclear development and a second weapons laboratory, but distinguishes that campaign from the work at Los Alamos that produced the tested devices.

people.name: Stanislaw Ulam
people.description: Quigley credits Ulam’s February 1951 suggestion with opening the successful route to thermonuclear development, alongside Teller’s subsequent presentation of the idea.

people.name: Paul H. Nitze
people.description: Quigley identifies Nitze’s policy-planning staff as the sponsor of NSC 68, a balanced defense strategy that conflicted with reliance on strategic bombing alone.

people.name: Dean Acheson
people.description: Quigley discusses Acheson’s 1950 Pacific defense-perimeter speech as a distinction between unilateral guarantees and collective defense, and later concessions to domestic anti-Communist pressure.

people.name: Douglas MacArthur
people.description: Quigley connects MacArthur’s Pacific defense perimeter, Korean command and dismissal with American strategic disagreements; he also discusses occupation policy in Japan.

people.name: Joseph Stalin
people.description: Quigley portrays Stalin’s rule through rival hierarchies of party, state, army and police, and treats his death as the opening of a five-year succession struggle.

people.name: Nikita Khrushchev
people.description: Quigley follows Khrushchev’s use of the party hierarchy, economic decentralization, de-Stalinization and support from the army to defeat rival leaders and acquire the premiership.

people.name: Georgi Malenkov
people.description: Quigley presents Malenkov as an early successor to Stalin whose retention of the premiership and surrender of party control helped Khrushchev outmaneuver him.

people.name: Lavrenti Beria
people.description: Quigley describes Beria’s security apparatus, initial post-Stalin relaxation and elimination by rival leaders aided by the regular army; the account acknowledges uncertainty about the execution date.

people.name: Vyacheslav Molotov
people.role: Soviet foreign minister and senior leader
people.description: Quigley depicts Molotov as a defender of Stalinist policies whose positions and authority were progressively removed by Khrushchev.

people.name: Nikolai Bulganin
people.description: Quigley describes Bulganin’s cooperation with Khrushchev in diplomatic visits and internal power struggles, followed by his replacement as premier in 1958.

people.name: Georgi Zhukov
people.description: Quigley gives the army and Zhukov a major role in Khrushchev’s survival during the 1957 leadership challenge, before Khrushchev removed him from defense and party posts.

people.name: Josip Broz Tito
people.description: Quigley treats Tito’s independent path to socialism as a challenge to Soviet control and connects the 1955 reconciliation with later upheaval among the East European satellites.

people.name: Imre Nagy
people.description: Quigley describes Nagy’s government during the 1956 Hungarian uprising, its declaration of neutrality, and the collapse under Soviet intervention.

people.name: János Kádár
people.description: Quigley describes Kádár’s shift from Nagy’s circle to a Soviet-backed government during the Hungarian uprising.

people.name: William Liscum Borden
people.description: Quigley describes Borden’s support for accelerated thermonuclear development and his 1953 letter to Hoover accusing Oppenheimer of being a Soviet agent. The book rejects the accusation’s framing.

people.name: Thomas J. Watson
people.description: Quigley recounts Watson’s role in the Columbia presidential search following Lamont’s death and presents the resulting Eisenhower appointment as an illustration of declining Morgan influence.

people.name: Nicholas Murray Butler
people.description: Quigley calls Butler an academic spokesman for Morgan interests and presents the prolonged difficulty of replacing him as evidence of changing power on Columbia’s trustees.

people.name: Frank C. Tiarks
people.description: Quigley identifies Tiarks as a Schroeder London partner and director of the Bank of England, Lazard Brothers and the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, connecting him with Allen Dulles’s banking associations.

people.name: H. Norman Schwarzkopf Sr.
people.role: Police official and Iranian gendarmerie adviser
people.description: Quigley places Schwarzkopf in training the Imperial Iranian Gendarmerie and in the financing and preparation of the 1953 anti-Mossadeq operation. This is the father of the later Gulf War commander.

people.name: Loy W. Henderson
people.description: Quigley names Henderson among visitors to Allen Dulles in Switzerland during the August 1953 operation against Mossadeq.

people.name: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
people.description: Quigley links the shah, the army and the conservative elite with Mossadeq’s overthrow, subsequent Western alignment and a later shift toward agrarian reform.

people.name: David Ben-Gurion
people.description: Quigley discusses Ben-Gurion’s role in the Zionist movement and his proclamation of the state of Israel in May 1948.

people.name: Muhammad Naguib
people.description: Quigley describes Naguib as the nominal head of the 1952 officers’ revolution and follows his displacement by Nasser during the consolidation of the new regime.

people.name: Farouk of Egypt
people.description: Quigley places Farouk’s monarchy amid land concentration, political discontent, British interference and army alienation, culminating in his 1952 deposition.

people.name: Hussein of Jordan
people.description: Quigley connects Hussein’s dismissal of Glubb, regional rivalries, and American and British assistance with the fragility of Jordan’s monarchy after Suez.

people.name: John Bagot Glubb
people.description: Quigley describes Glubb as the British officer who trained and commanded Jordan’s Arab Legion; his dismissal in 1956 weakened a chief connection between Britain and the Jordanian monarchy.

people.name: Dag Hammarskjöld
people.description: Quigley credits Hammarskjöld’s 1958 Near Eastern mission with helping evacuate American and British troops from Lebanon and Jordan.

people.name: Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán
people.description: Quigley relates Árbenz’s land reform to conflict with United Fruit and the CIA-supported 1954 overthrow. The author distinguishes the exile attack from the Guatemalan army’s decisive role.

people.name: Carlos Castillo Armas
people.description: Quigley describes Castillo Armas as American-trained and financed, leading exiles from Honduras and Nicaragua in the CIA-directed 1954 assault.

people.name: Anastas Mikoyan
people.description: Quigley follows Mikoyan through the Soviet succession struggle and identifies his 1960 Cuban visit with a sugar-for-petroleum-and-arms agreement.

people.name: Charles de Gaulle
people.description: Quigley links de Gaulle’s return with the Algerian crisis and follows his efforts to reduce France’s dependence on NATO and retain cooperation with former African colonies.

people.name: Mao Zedong
people.description: Quigley connects Mao’s nuclear requests and the Great Leap Forward with China’s resource constraints and deteriorating relations with the Soviet Union.

people.name: Kwame Nkrumah
people.description: Quigley discusses Nkrumah’s educational connections, party-building, Ghana’s independence and Pan-African initiatives, while criticizing his subsequent concentration of power.

people.name: Ahmed Sékou Touré
people.description: Quigley describes Touré’s rejection of the French Community constitution, French retaliation and Guinea’s search for alternative support.

people.name: George Padmore
people.description: Quigley credits Padmore with organizing an independent-African-states initiative for Nkrumah, linking Pan-African ideas with the Accra meeting of 1958.

people.name: Félix Houphouët-Boigny
people.description: Quigley identifies Houphouët-Boigny as an organizer of the French-centered African grouping called the Brazzaville Twelve.

people.name: David Ormsby-Gore, fifth Baron Harlech
people.description: Quigley uses the Kennedy family’s connection with the British Embassy as an illustration of Atlantic Establishment ties. He identifies David as the son of William Ormsby-Gore, an associate of Milner and Amery; the two are distinct people.

people.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
people.role: United States president and former Columbia president
people.description: Quigley connects Eisenhower’s Columbia appointment with the declining influence of Morgan interests on its trustees. As president, Eisenhower appears in the New Look’s budget and nuclear-strategy changes, the Geneva summit and open-skies proposal; the book distinguishes his outlook from that of Dulles and the Republican congressional right.

people.name: Mohammad Mossadeq
people.description: Quigley describes Mossadeq carrying out oil nationalization after his appointment in 1951 and facing British company resistance, changing American policy and the international petroleum cartel. The book attributes his 1953 overthrow to a combination of CIA action, the shah, army elements and conservative interests, while discussing his unsuccessful reliance on street support against military opponents.

people.name: Fulgencio Batista
people.description: Quigley follows Batista from his overthrow of Grau San Martín through rule by civilian intermediaries and a later return to power in March 1952. The book connects the regime’s violence and corruption with declining military and middle-class support and the rise of Castro’s guerrilla movement.

people.name: John F. Kennedy
people.description: Quigley describes Kennedy accepting CIA assurances before the Bay of Pigs invasion, then managing the 1962 missile crisis as a direct Soviet-American confrontation. In the late-book social analysis, the author also places Kennedy within an informal Atlantic Establishment through support for Britain and connections with the British Embassy and the Ormsby-Gore family; this is an interpretation of influence, not formal membership.

people.name: Allen W. Dulles
people.role: CIA director and former banking director
people.description: Quigley identifies Allen Dulles as CIA director during the Iranian and Guatemalan interventions and the agency’s Cuba invasion planning. His discussion of Iran connects Dulles’s former Schroeder Bank directorship in New York with Frank Tiarks’s London banking and Anglo-Iranian Oil Company positions, while retaining these associations as contextual evidence in the author’s account.

people.name: Fidel Castro
people.description: Quigley traces Castro’s movement from the failed 1953 revolt through guerrilla warfare, the 1959 regime transition and an early reform program. He then follows expanding Soviet economic and military ties, the consequences of the Bay of Pigs defeat and Castro’s resentment at being bypassed in the missile-crisis settlement.

people.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
people.description: Quigley describes Nasser as the effective leader of the officers’ conspiracy behind Egypt’s 1952 revolution and follows his displacement of Naguib and consolidation of authority. The book links agrarian reform, cotton-for-arms commitments, Aswan Dam financing, Suez nationalization and the Egyptian-Syrian union, while criticizing Nasser’s regional ambitions and authoritarian methods.

people.name: J. Edgar Hoover
people.description: Quigley names Hoover as recipient of William Liscum Borden’s November 1953 letter accusing Oppenheimer of probable Soviet agency. The book criticizes the accusation and connects it with the subsequent security-clearance action; this passage does not establish that Hoover originated the accusation or independently proved it.

organizations.name: United States Atomic Energy Commission
organizations.description: Civilian nuclear commission financing detection and weapons development, with advisory scientists and commissioners in conflict over thermonuclear, tactical and defensive priorities in Quigley’s account.

organizations.name: AEC General Advisory Committee
organizations.description: Scientific advisory committee to the Atomic Energy Commission; Quigley describes its 1949 opposition to a crash hydrogen-bomb program and its support for a broader defense response.

organizations.name: United States National Security Council
organizations.description: Federal strategic policy body that reviewed defense planning and accepted directives NSC 68 and NSC 162 in Quigley’s account.

organizations.name: United States Air Force
organizations.description: American armed service whose strategic-bombing interests Quigley contrasts with ground-force needs, tactical nuclear development and continental air defense.

organizations.name: Strategic Air Command
organizations.description: Air Force command associated with strategic nuclear bombing. Quigley presents its institutional interests as a major force in disputes over weapons diversification and air-defense spending.

organizations.name: Los Alamos weapons laboratory
organizations.description: Nuclear weapons laboratory whose postwar work under Norris Bradbury produced tested thermonuclear devices; Quigley distinguishes its achievements from Teller’s advocacy.

organizations.name: Livermore weapons laboratory
organizations.description: Second weapons laboratory associated with Lawrence’s Berkeley Radiation Laboratory, established in July 1952 after Teller sought Air Force support.

organizations.name: MIT Lincoln Laboratory
organizations.description: Air-defense research laboratory established in September 1951, associated with radar warning and integrated interception proposals.

organizations.name: United Nations
organizations.description: International organization whose collective-security machinery, mediation and emergency forces appear throughout Quigley’s postwar account; the Korean intervention relied on the Soviet absence from the Security Council.

organizations.name: North Atlantic Treaty Organization
organizations.description: Atlantic defense alliance. Quigley places NATO in both the balanced-defense strategy of NSC 68 and Dulles’s later network of regional treaty barriers.

organizations.name: Southeast Asia Treaty Organization
organizations.description: Regional defense arrangement signed in 1954 by eight states, treated by Quigley as a portion of Dulles’s perimeter around the Soviet bloc.

organizations.name: Baghdad Pact / Central Treaty Organization
organizations.description: Regional treaty arrangement formed in 1955 by Britain, Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Pakistan; Quigley describes the 1959 renaming after Iraq withdrew.

organizations.name: Warsaw Pact
organizations.description: Soviet-bloc military alliance whose authority was challenged by Hungary’s 1956 declaration of withdrawal and neutrality.

organizations.name: Communist Party of the Soviet Union
organizations.description: Party hierarchy which Quigley regards as the decisive instrument of Khrushchev’s rise, contrasting it with the state ministries and the security apparatus.

organizations.name: Columbia University
organizations.description: University whose trustees and presidential succession Quigley uses to illustrate Morgan influence and its postwar weakening.

organizations.name: International Business Machines
organizations.description: Corporation led by Thomas Watson, whom Quigley names as chairman of Columbia’s presidential search committee after Lamont’s death.

organizations.name: Schroeder Bank, New York
organizations.description: Bank of which Quigley identifies Allen Dulles as a former director; this is a distinct institution from the London and Cologne banking connections named nearby.

organizations.name: Schroeder Bank, London
organizations.description: Banking partnership with which Quigley associates Frank Tiarks from 1902; the book connects Tiarks with AIOC and other British financial institutions.

organizations.name: Imperial Iranian Gendarmerie
organizations.description: Iranian policing force trained by H. Norman Schwarzkopf in Quigley’s account of the 1953 operation against Mossadeq.

organizations.name: Suez Canal Company
organizations.description: Canal operating company nationalized by Nasser in 1956; Quigley discusses its ownership, profits, pilots and the dispute over Egyptian versus international control.

organizations.name: Egyptian Free Officers
organizations.description: Officers’ conspiratorial group behind the 1952 revolution, described by Quigley as centered on Nasser and drawn from the military academy generation of 1938.

organizations.name: Arab Legion
organizations.description: Jordanian armed force trained and commanded by British officers including Glubb; Quigley treats it as a major support of the monarchy.

organizations.name: United Nations Emergency Force
organizations.description: Force sent to supervise evacuation of Egyptian territory and Gaza following the Suez crisis in Quigley’s account.

organizations.name: United Arab Republic
organizations.description: Egyptian-Syrian political union established in February 1958 and broken by Syria after a 1961 coup.

organizations.name: United Fruit Company
organizations.description: American enterprise whose uncultivated Guatemalan land was affected by Árbenz’s reform. Quigley connects this dispute with American intervention.

organizations.name: Organization of American States
organizations.description: Hemispheric organization through which Dulles obtained a declaration against Guatemala and which supported the American quarantine of Cuba in 1962.

organizations.name: July 26 Movement
organizations.description: Castro’s revolutionary movement, whose initial middle-class leadership and early reform program Quigley distinguishes from later Communist administrative control.

organizations.name: Chinese Communist Party
organizations.description: Party ruling mainland China, whose role in agricultural communes, economic management and the Sino-Soviet dispute Quigley discusses.

organizations.name: Convention People’s Party
organizations.description: Ghanaian political party founded and controlled by Nkrumah; its 1951 electoral victory led to his release from prison and assumption of government.

organizations.name: Union of African and Malagasy States / Brazzaville Twelve
organizations.description: French-centered African grouping which Quigley contrasts with Nkrumah’s Pan-African initiatives; it coordinated diplomacy and technical cooperation.

organizations.name: Union of African States
organizations.description: Association of Ghana, Guinea and Mali in Quigley’s account, reflecting Nkrumah’s efforts at Pan-African union and competition with other African groupings.

organizations.name: Eastern Establishment — Quigley’s analytical grouping
organizations.description: Quigley’s description of an informal Atlantic elite associated with older Wall Street wealth, Ivy League institutions, foundations and Anglophile internationalism. This is an analytical grouping, not a formal membership organization.

organizations.name: Anglo-Iranian Oil Company / BP
organizations.description: Quigley describes AIOC’s resistance to Iranian oil nationalization, withdrawal of technical staff and connection with the international petroleum cartel. He lists Frank Tiarks among its directors and describes the post-coup consortium settlement retaining a 40 percent AIOC interest.

organizations.name: Central Intelligence Agency
organizations.description: Quigley attributes major roles in the Iranian and Guatemalan interventions and the Bay of Pigs operation to the CIA under Allen Dulles. He argues that the agency misread its Guatemala experience and mishandled Cuban planning, local opposition relationships, air power and logistics.

organizations.name: Seven Sisters oil cartel
organizations.description: Quigley describes a world oil cartel developing from a 1928 agreement among Royal Dutch-Shell, Anglo-Iranian and Standard Oil and encompassing seven major companies by 1949. He connects its pricing and marketing interests with resistance to Iranian nationalization and the later consortium settlement; the cartel is an intercompany arrangement rather than a conventional membership society.

organizations.name: United States Department of State
organizations.description: Quigley places State Department policy planning under Paul Nitze behind NSC 68 and describes Acheson’s Pacific defense speech. Under John Foster Dulles, the department appears in massive retaliation, regional treaties, Japan’s peace settlement and the diplomatic confrontation with Guatemala, illustrating competing postwar policy directions.

organizations.name: United States Department of Defense
organizations.description: Quigley discusses the defense establishment’s competing requirements for ground troops, tactical air support, nuclear weapons and continental protection. The Korean War, scientific defense projects and Eisenhower’s New Look connect departmental resources and strategic plans with rival armed-service interests and fiscal limits.

organizations.name: Joint Chiefs of Staff
organizations.description: Quigley describes the Joint Chiefs pressing for accelerated hydrogen-bomb work, participating in Pacific strategic assessments and developing proposals incorporated in the New Look. The book also records their approval of the Bay of Pigs plan before Kennedy accepted the invasion.

organizations.name: Cuban exile executive committee · unnamed in supplied PDF
organizations.description: Quigley describes an executive committee of Cuban refugees in the United States, contrasts it with reform-minded anti-Castro groups inside Cuba and says the CIA excluded it from planning and detained its leaders during the invasion. The PDF does not give a formal institutional name, so it is not equated with a named council in another source.

organizations.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation
organizations.description: Quigley identifies the FBI through Borden’s November 1953 letter to Hoover accusing Oppenheimer of being a Soviet agent. The source uses this communication in tracing the clearance controversy, without establishing the agency’s independent validation of the allegation.

events.name: Eisenhower chosen as Columbia president in Quigley’s Morgan-succession account
events.summary: Quigley recounts the selection of Dwight Eisenhower as Columbia president after Thomas Lamont’s death. Thomas Watson chaired the search, following a long struggle over replacing Nicholas Murray Butler. The episode is presented as evidence that Morgan interests could obstruct a succession without still controlling its outcome.
details: Quigley recounts the selection of Dwight Eisenhower as Columbia president after Thomas Lamont’s death. Thomas Watson chaired the search, following a long struggle over replacing Nicholas Murray Butler. The episode is presented as evidence that Morgan interests could obstruct a succession without still controlling its outcome.

The story connects corporate leadership, university trustees and national politics rather than treating Columbia as an isolated academic institution. Quigley attributes the appointment partly to Watson’s misunderstanding of a suggestion referring to Milton Eisenhower; that anecdote is preserved as the author’s account, rather than asserted as an independently established explanation.
events.context: The story connects corporate leadership, university trustees and national politics rather than treating Columbia as an isolated academic institution.

events.name: Truman announces a Soviet atomic explosion
events.summary: Quigley describes airborne monitoring detecting radioactive material from a Soviet explosion in August 1949. Truman publicly announced the finding on September 23. The event ended assumptions of an enduring American atomic monopoly and brought existing arguments over thermonuclear development and armed-service strategy to a crisis.
details: Quigley describes airborne monitoring detecting radioactive material from a Soviet explosion in August 1949. Truman publicly announced the finding on September 23. The event ended assumptions of an enduring American atomic monopoly and brought existing arguments over thermonuclear development and armed-service strategy to a crisis.

The commission had sponsored a continuous atmospheric-monitoring program following a suggestion from Lewis Strauss. Detection therefore linked scientific surveillance with strategic policy: the explosion’s importance lay not only in Soviet technical achievement but in the American institutional decisions it forced into the open.
events.context: The commission had sponsored a continuous atmospheric-monitoring program following a suggestion from Lewis Strauss.

events.name: AEC advisers oppose a crash hydrogen-bomb program
events.summary: The AEC General Advisory Committee unanimously opposed a crash hydrogen-bomb program in October 1949, according to Quigley. The advisers preferred diversified atomic weapons, stronger ground forces and reorganized European defense. Their opposition concerned scientific feasibility, allocation of reactors and trained personnel, and the strategic usefulness of larger weapons.

The advisers preferred diversified atomic weapons, stronger ground forces and reorganized European defense. Their opposition concerned scientific feasibility, allocation of reactors and trained personnel, and the strategic usefulness of larger weapons.

Quigley contrasts the committee’s position with Teller, congressional supporters and the Air Force. The disagreement is an argument over competing defense systems and resource allocation. The author does not present scientific opposition to the hydrogen bomb as evidence of disloyalty or Soviet allegiance.
events.context: Quigley contrasts the committee’s position with Teller, congressional supporters and the Air Force. The disagreement is an argument over competing defense systems and resource allocation.

events.name: Acheson defines unilateral and collective Pacific defense
events.summary: Acheson’s January 12 speech accepted a Pacific defense perimeter associated with MacArthur, excluding Korea and Formosa from an explicit unilateral American guarantee. Quigley stresses that Acheson still envisaged collective defense through the United Nations west of that line, rather than declaring those areas categorically undefended.

Quigley stresses that Acheson still envisaged collective defense through the United Nations west of that line, rather than declaring those areas categorically undefended.

The distinction matters to the author’s later discussion of partisan accusations over Korea. Quigley places the speech in a broader expectation that Chinese Nationalist power would disappear and that diplomacy might exploit eventual friction between Communist China and the Soviet Union.

events.name: Truman orders thermonuclear work and a strategic review
events.summary: Quigley describes Truman’s decision as a triple order: continue work toward a hydrogen bomb, continue developing varied atomic weapons, and undertake a National Security Council review of strategic plans. He argues that later accounts misleadingly reduced the decision to an isolated crash hydrogen-bomb instruction.
details: Quigley describes Truman’s decision as a triple order: continue work toward a hydrogen bomb, continue developing varied atomic weapons, and undertake a National Security Council review of strategic plans. He argues that later accounts misleadingly reduced the decision to an isolated crash hydrogen-bomb instruction.

The order connected weapons laboratories, reactor construction and broader defense strategy. Quigley follows it with pressure from the Joint Chiefs for acceleration and expansion of production facilities, placing thermonuclear work within the contest between strategic bombing and a diversified military response.

Quigley follows it with pressure from the Joint Chiefs for acceleration and expansion of production facilities, placing thermonuclear work within the contest between strategic bombing and a diversified military response.

events.name: National Security Council accepts NSC 68
events.summary: Quigley identifies Paul Nitze’s State Department policy-planning staff as the sponsor of NSC 68, accepted in April 1950. It anticipated a strategic nuclear stalemate and advocated strengthened ground forces, allied defense and tactical nuclear weapons rather than exclusive reliance on strategic bombing.

It anticipated a strategic nuclear stalemate and advocated strengthened ground forces, allied defense and tactical nuclear weapons rather than exclusive reliance on strategic bombing.

The author places the directive in direct tension with Air Force interests and its eventual replacement by the Eisenhower administration’s New Look. This is a policy connection between NATO’s defense needs, American budget decisions and the weapons diversification favored by Oppenheimer’s advisers.
events.context: The author places the directive in direct tension with Air Force interests and its eventual replacement by the Eisenhower administration’s New Look.

events.name: North Korean attack opens the Korean War
events.summary: Quigley describes North Korean troops crossing the 38th parallel on June 25, rapidly driving the lightly equipped South Korean forces toward Pusan. Truman’s response committed air and naval power and sought United Nations condemnation, transforming a regional invasion into a test of collective security.
details: Quigley describes North Korean troops crossing the 38th parallel on June 25, rapidly driving the lightly equipped South Korean forces toward Pusan. Truman’s response committed air and naval power and sought United Nations condemnation, transforming a regional invasion into a test of collective security.

The Soviet delegation was absent from the Security Council in protest over Nationalist China’s representation. Quigley treats that absence as critical because it removed the Soviet veto from the decisions authorizing assistance to South Korea. The event intersects military operations and international institutions.
events.context: The Soviet delegation was absent from the Security Council in protest over Nationalist China’s representation.

events.name: United Nations calls for assistance to South Korea
events.summary: Quigley dates the Security Council’s condemnation and request for assistance to South Korea to June 27,1950. On the same day Truman ordered American forces into action and sent the Seventh Fleet into the Formosa Strait, broadening the policy consequences beyond the Korean peninsula.
details: Quigley dates the Security Council’s condemnation and request for assistance to South Korea to June 27,1950. On the same day Truman ordered American forces into action and sent the Seventh Fleet into the Formosa Strait, broadening the policy consequences beyond the Korean peninsula.

The author describes the vote as an unprecedented use of a world organization’s collective force against aggression. Soviet absence enabled it, while the American naval move also changed relations between Washington, mainland China and Chiang Kai-shek’s regime.
events.context: The author describes the vote as an unprecedented use of a world organization’s collective force against aggression.

events.name: Ulam’s suggestion opens the successful thermonuclear route
events.summary: Quigley credits a suggestion made by Stanislaw Ulam to Teller in February 1951 with opening the successful thermonuclear approach. Teller presented the developed idea to the General Advisory Committee in June, where the scientists recognized that a workable route had emerged.
details: Quigley credits a suggestion made by Stanislaw Ulam to Teller in February 1951 with opening the successful thermonuclear approach. Teller presented the developed idea to the General Advisory Committee in June, where the scientists recognized that a workable route had emerged.

The account distinguishes the eventual solution from Teller’s earlier 1946–1951 program. This distinction underlies Quigley’s criticism of the public narrative assigning Teller sole credit and portraying scientific or administration opposition as having simply delayed an already viable weapon.

This distinction underlies Quigley’s criticism of the public narrative assigning Teller sole credit and portraying scientific or administration opposition as having simply delayed an already viable weapon.

events.name: Dulles obtains a peace treaty for Japan
events.summary: Quigley credits Dulles with obtaining the Japanese peace treaty of September 8,1951, after he was brought into State Department work under Truman. The appointment occurred amid domestic pressure over China and the Korean War, which had prompted concessions to anti-Communist critics.
details: Quigley credits Dulles with obtaining the Japanese peace treaty of September 8,1951, after he was brought into State Department work under Truman. The appointment occurred amid domestic pressure over China and the Korean War, which had prompted concessions to anti-Communist critics.

The author connects Dulles’s diplomatic career with his earlier Wall Street and Sullivan and Cromwell associations, then describes a shift toward unilateralism and neo-isolationist rhetoric. The treaty belongs to that transition between establishment connections and the policies Dulles pursued under Eisenhower.
events.context: The author connects Dulles’s diplomatic career with his earlier Wall Street and Sullivan and Cromwell associations, then describes a shift toward unilateralism and neo-isolationist rhetoric.

events.name: MIT establishes Lincoln Laboratory for air-defense research
events.summary: Quigley describes Lincoln Laboratory’s establishment at MIT in September 1951 following Project Charles. Related studies examined radar warning, interception and automatic communications because existing defenses could not reliably stop enough attacking aircraft to be acceptable in nuclear warfare.
details: Quigley describes Lincoln Laboratory’s establishment at MIT in September 1951 following Project Charles. Related studies examined radar warning, interception and automatic communications because existing defenses could not reliably stop enough attacking aircraft to be acceptable in nuclear warfare.

The laboratory illustrates a conflict inside the defense establishment: the Air Force instigated research but resisted expensive defensive recommendations that competed with strategic-bomber spending. Quigley relates these disputes to the later attack on Oppenheimer and other advocates of diversified defense.
events.context: The laboratory illustrates a conflict inside the defense establishment: the Air Force instigated research but resisted expensive defensive recommendations that competed with strategic-bomber spending.

events.name: Cairo fires deepen the Egyptian political crisis
events.summary: Quigley links the Cairo fires of January 26,1952, with a preceding clash over British attempts to disarm Egyptian police in the Canal Zone. Police and army refused to suppress the incendiaries, while Farouk dismissed Nahas and failed to find a government capable of restoring confidence.
details: Quigley links the Cairo fires of January 26,1952, with a preceding clash over British attempts to disarm Egyptian police in the Canal Zone. Police and army refused to suppress the incendiaries, while Farouk dismissed Nahas and failed to find a government capable of restoring confidence.

The author presents the riots as destructive to the political system even though they were not the officers’ planned revolution. They widened the opening for a small military conspiracy already shaped by British interference, the monarchy’s conduct and humiliation in the 1948 war.
events.context: The author presents the riots as destructive to the political system even though they were not the officers’ planned revolution.

events.name: Second weapons laboratory established at Livermore
events.summary: Quigley dates Livermore Laboratory’s establishment to July 1952, following Teller’s departure from Los Alamos and lobbying for a second weapons laboratory. After initial AEC resistance, Teller obtained Air Force support for the new institution attached to Lawrence’s Radiation Laboratory.
details: Quigley dates Livermore Laboratory’s establishment to July 1952, following Teller’s departure from Los Alamos and lobbying for a second weapons laboratory. After initial AEC resistance, Teller obtained Air Force support for the new institution attached to Lawrence’s Radiation Laboratory.

The author distinguishes institutional creation from credit for the thermonuclear tests already being developed at Los Alamos. In his account, the laboratory’s formation shows how scientists could ally with a military service in disputes over control of weapons development and competing strategic priorities.

events.name: Egyptian officers seize state and army institutions

events.name: Egyptian junta adopts an agrarian law
events.summary: Quigley describes the September 1952 agrarian law as an attempt to limit large estates, transfer surplus land to working peasants and redirect landlord wealth into industry and commerce. events.name: Operation Ivy tests a thermonuclear device at Eniwetok
events.summary: Quigley dates the Mike test at Eniwetok to November 1,1952, and describes a roughly ten-megaton explosion that destroyed its test islet. He emphasizes that the enormous refrigerated apparatus demonstrated thermonuclear feasibility but was not yet a practical aircraft-delivered bomb.

events.name: Stalin’s death opens a Soviet succession struggle
events.summary: Quigley describes Stalin’s death on March 5,1953, as interrupting preparations for another purge. events.name: Korean armistice ends 37 months of war
events.summary: Quigley dates the Korean truce to July 27,1953, after Stalin’s death and the arrival of the Eisenhower administration helped break a prolonged stalemate. events.name: Nasser replaces Naguib as Egyptian prime minister

events.name: Egypt and Syria establish the United Arab Republic
events.summary: Quigley describes Egypt and Syria uniting as the United Arab Republic in February 1958, after an economic-union agreement and Soviet-bloc lending to Syria. Iraq and Jordan responded with a short-lived federation, while rival Arab states remained deeply divided despite language of common nationalism.

Iraq and Jordan responded with a short-lived federation, while rival Arab states remained deeply divided despite language of common nationalism.

The author follows the union into Syria’s 1961 withdrawal after a military coup, using its brief existence to question assumptions that the Arab world constituted a durable unified power bloc. The timeline retains the source’s month-level precision rather than inferring an exact proclamation date.

events.name: Khrushchev adds the Soviet premiership to party leadership
events.summary: Quigley connects the new Supreme Soviet’s assembly on March 28,1958, with Bulganin’s resignation and Khrushchev’s replacement of him as premier. Khrushchev now held leadership of both state and party, completing the consolidation begun after Stalin’s death.

The author emphasizes that Khrushchev’s power rested more heavily on the party hierarchy than Stalin’s later rule had. Bulganin’s eventual expulsion illustrates how cooperation during the rise did not preserve a subordinate’s influence once the remaining offices were absorbed.

events.precisionNote: Date anchors the source’s March 28 assembly; the passage associates the premiership change with that proceeding.

events.name: Accra meeting advances Padmore and Nkrumah’s Pan-African initiative
events.summary: Quigley describes the first Accra meeting of independent African states in April 1958 as organized by George Padmore for Nkrumah. Representatives of eight independent states demanded an end to French military operations in Algeria and independence for remaining African territories.
details: Quigley describes the first Accra meeting of independent African states in April 1958 as organized by George Padmore for Nkrumah. Representatives of eight independent states demanded an end to French military operations in Algeria and independence for remaining African territories.

The author connects the initiative with subsequent meetings and anti-apartheid activity, but notes resistance to an immediate United States of Africa. It was one strand in a developing competition among Pan-African schemes rather than a single organization encompassing all future independent African governments.
events.context: The author connects the initiative with subsequent meetings and anti-apartheid activity, but notes resistance to an immediate United States of Africa.

events.name: American forces land in Lebanon after the Iraqi coup
events.summary: Quigley describes American landings in Lebanon during July 15–17,1958, following the overthrow of Iraq’s monarchy and fears for Lebanon’s government. Britain also sent a parachute brigade to Jordan at Hussein’s request. A United Nations mission later helped evacuate both deployments.

The author emphasizes that a UN commission found no evidence of outside forces subverting Lebanon during the same week. He uses the episode to criticize policies that interpreted regional instability as Communist penetration and to connect the post-Suez power vacuum with Cold War intervention.
events.context: The author emphasizes that a UN commission found no evidence of outside forces subverting Lebanon during the same week.

events.name: China’s Great Leap Forward reorganizes communes and economic control
events.summary: Quigley describes the 1958 Great Leap Forward as merging hundreds of thousands of collective farms into large communes that controlled work, education, child care and social life. The goal was to extract greater agricultural surpluses and release labor for industry through drastic changes in rural organization.
details: Quigley describes the 1958 Great Leap Forward as merging hundreds of thousands of collective farms into large communes that controlled work, education, child care and social life. The goal was to extract greater agricultural surpluses and release labor for industry through drastic changes in rural organization.

The author relates the program to subsequent food shortages, industrial contraction and foreign-exchange pressure. His account connects domestic economic strategy with more aggressive Chinese foreign policy and the weakening Sino-Soviet relationship, while estimates and judgments remain attributed to the book.
events.context: The author relates the program to subsequent food shortages, industrial contraction and foreign-exchange pressure.

events.name: Guinea rejects the French Community and seeks alternative aid
events.summary: Quigley describes Guinea rejecting the 1958 French Community constitution under Sékou Touré. De Gaulle withdrew political and financial support, and Guinea sought Soviet assistance, accepted a loan through union with Ghana and tried to establish alternatives to the French economic connection.
details: Quigley describes Guinea rejecting the 1958 French Community constitution under Sékou Touré. De Gaulle withdrew political and financial support, and Guinea sought Soviet assistance, accepted a loan through union with Ghana and tried to establish alternatives to the French economic connection.

The author follows Guinea’s mixture of nationalization, foreign recognition and aid-seeking before its later effort to work back toward French Africa. This trajectory links anti-colonial sovereignty to continuing dependence on outside development resources and competition between the superpowers.
events.context: The author follows Guinea’s mixture of nationalization, foreign recognition and aid-seeking before its later effort to work back toward French Africa.

events.name: Khrushchev threatens transfer of Berlin access rights
events.summary: Quigley describes Khrushchev’s November 27 note demanding a Berlin settlement within six months. The Soviet Union threatened a separate treaty with East Germany and transfer of its rights, including Allied access routes, to a regime the Western powers did not recognize.
details: Quigley describes Khrushchev’s November 27 note demanding a Berlin settlement within six months. The Soviet Union threatened a separate treaty with East Germany and transfer of its rights, including Allied access routes, to a regime the Western powers did not recognize.

The author links the ultimatum with Soviet confidence in its missile image and with the practical problem of compelling Western recognition of East Germany. The crisis developed alongside fractures within both blocs, particularly French objections to American unilateral actions and Chinese dissatisfaction with Soviet assistance.
events.context: The author links the ultimatum with Soviet confidence in its missile image and with the practical problem of compelling Western recognition of East Germany.

events.name: Castro’s victory replaces Batista’s government
events.summary: Quigley places the revolutionary victory at New Year 1959, following guerrilla operations begun in late 1956 and erosion of Batista’s military and middle-class support. He describes an initial program of schools, health centers, reduced rents, land reform and wider access to public amenities.
details: Quigley places the revolutionary victory at New Year 1959, following guerrilla operations begun in late 1956 and erosion of Batista’s military and middle-class support. He describes an initial program of schools, health centers, reduced rents, land reform and wider access to public amenities.

The author distinguishes those early reforms from subsequent executions, permanent-revolution claims and growing Communist administrative influence. The date anchors the transition of regimes; the book’s statement about Castro personally entering Havana on New Year’s Day is not reproduced as a precise movement record.
events.context: The author distinguishes those early reforms from subsequent executions, permanent-revolution claims and growing Communist administrative influence.
events.precisionNote: Date marks the source’s New Year 1959 regime transition, not an independently verified date for Castro’s personal arrival in Havana.

events.name: Mikoyan’s visit binds Cuban sugar to Soviet supplies
events.summary: Quigley describes Mikoyan’s February 1960 visit to Cuba and an agreement exchanging sugar for Soviet petroleum, arms and other supplies. It was followed by diplomatic relations, conflict over American-owned refineries processing Soviet crude and escalating sugar-quota and nationalization disputes.
details: Quigley describes Mikoyan’s February 1960 visit to Cuba and an agreement exchanging sugar for Soviet petroleum, arms and other supplies. It was followed by diplomatic relations, conflict over American-owned refineries processing Soviet crude and escalating sugar-quota and nationalization disputes.

The author interprets the commitment of the main export crop as an economic trap similar to Egypt’s cotton-for-arms arrangement. He links Cuba’s growing reliance on the Soviet bloc with the deterioration of American relations and the later decision to attempt Castro’s removal by force.
events.context: The author interprets the commitment of the main export crop as an economic trap similar to Egypt’s cotton-for-arms arrangement.

events.name: Soviet Union withdraws advisers from China
events.summary: Quigley describes the withdrawal of almost all Soviet technical and military advisers during summer 1960 as a major step in the Sino-Soviet deterioration. China’s agricultural crisis and debt obligations already constrained its ability to import equipment and sustain development.
details: Quigley describes the withdrawal of almost all Soviet technical and military advisers during summer 1960 as a major step in the Sino-Soviet deterioration. China’s agricultural crisis and debt obligations already constrained its ability to import equipment and sustain development.

The author argues that the withdrawal could not be explained as routine business practice. He locates it within deeper disputes over resources, regional priorities, national development stages and Soviet accommodation with the United States, separating those structural causes from a single ideological quarrel.
events.context: The author argues that the withdrawal could not be explained as routine business practice. He locates it within deeper disputes over resources, regional priorities, national development stages and Soviet accommodation with the United States, separating those structural causes from a single ideological quarrel.
events.precisionNote: Source gives summer1960 only; year precision preserves the uncertainty and January1 is a display anchor, not a claimed day.

events.name: Bay of Pigs invasion fails within seventy-two hours
events.summary: Quigley dates the landing of 1,500 men at the Bay of Pigs to April 17,1961. He describes CIA financing, training and control, Joint Chiefs approval and Kennedy’s acceptance of assurances that a landing would trigger resistance to Castro before Soviet armaments became fully operational.
details: Quigley dates the landing of 1,500 men at the Bay of Pigs to April 17,1961. He describes CIA financing, training and control, Joint Chiefs approval and Kennedy’s acceptance of assurances that a landing would trigger resistance to Castro before Soviet armaments became fully operational.

The author argues that planners misread the Guatemala precedent, alienated reform-minded opponents inside Cuba, withheld information from the underground and mishandled air power and logistics. The defeat strengthened Castro’s regional prestige and deepened Soviet commitment, forming an explicit bridge toward the missile crisis.
events.context: The author argues that planners misread the Guatemala precedent, alienated reform-minded opponents inside Cuba, withheld information from the underground and mishandled air power and logistics.
events.precisionNote: PDF p 942 explicitly gives April 17,1961; nearby p 938 incorrectly calls the invasion 1962. This entry follows the detailed event passage.

events.name: De Gaulle and Algerian rebels reach an independence settlement
events.summary: Quigley dates agreement between the Algerian rebels and de Gaulle’s government to March 18,1962, after years of war and violence that continued beyond the settlement. He connects the crisis with European settler interests, Algeria’s constitutional status and an army unwilling to accept another colonial defeat.
details: Quigley dates agreement between the Algerian rebels and de Gaulle’s government to March 18,1962, after years of war and violence that continued beyond the settlement. He connects the crisis with European settler interests, Algeria’s constitutional status and an army unwilling to accept another colonial defeat.

The author treats the 1958 return of de Gaulle and replacement of the Fourth Republic as consequences of the same conflict. The settlement therefore intersects decolonization with domestic constitutional change and the competing claims of military and civilian authority.
events.context: The author treats the 1958 return of de Gaulle and replacement of the Fourth Republic as consequences of the same conflict.

events.name: Kennedy announces the quarantine during the Cuban missile crisis
events.summary: Quigley describes Kennedy’s October 22 announcement of a naval quarantine after discovery of Soviet missile construction in Cuba. The crisis combined military mobilization, appeals to international institutions and uncertainty over whether Soviet ships would challenge the interception line.
details: Quigley describes Kennedy’s October 22 announcement of a naval quarantine after discovery of Soviet missile construction in Cuba. The crisis combined military mobilization, appeals to international institutions and uncertainty over whether Soviet ships would challenge the interception line.

The author treats the subsequent settlement as exposing the rivalry’s underlying power balance and both leaders’ aversion to thermonuclear war. Castro resisted inspection and resented being bypassed, illustrating how a superpower agreement could also strain relations with the smaller state at its center.
events.context: The author treats the subsequent settlement as exposing the rivalry’s underlying power balance and both leaders’ aversion to thermonuclear war.

events.name: Test Ban Treaty formalizes a superpower common interest
events.summary: Quigley identifies the August 1963 Test Ban Treaty as the first formal agreement expressing a shared interest made visible by the peaceful missile-crisis settlement. He interprets limits on testing as both preserving the superpower stalemate and obstructing the spread of nuclear weapons to additional powers.
details: Quigley identifies the August 1963 Test Ban Treaty as the first formal agreement expressing a shared interest made visible by the peaceful missile-crisis settlement. He interprets limits on testing as both preserving the superpower stalemate and obstructing the spread of nuclear weapons to additional powers.

The author places the treaty within a movement away from Dulles’s two-bloc picture toward multiple blocs and overlapping interests. In this interpretation the superpowers could cooperate in nuclear restraint even while disagreeing elsewhere, because uncontrolled proliferation threatened both of them.
events.context: The author places the treaty within a movement away from Dulles’s two-bloc picture toward multiple blocs and overlapping interests.

events.name: Brazzaville Twelve organize a French-centered African grouping
events.summary: Quigley describes the Brazzaville meeting of December 1960 as consolidating twelve former French African territories into a loose structure for cooperation and coordinated diplomacy. Houphouët-Boigny played a leading role, while earlier UN voting coordination and technical organizations provided practical instruments.
details: Quigley describes the Brazzaville meeting of December 1960 as consolidating twelve former French African territories into a loose structure for cooperation and coordinated diplomacy. Houphouët-Boigny played a leading role, while earlier UN voting coordination and technical organizations provided practical instruments.

The author contrasts the group’s cautious economic and social cooperation with Nkrumah’s more ambitious and contentious Pan-African schemes. A subsequent charter, specialist organizations and a shared budget gave the grouping an institutional existence beyond occasional declarations of political solidarity.
events.context: The author contrasts the group’s cautious economic and social cooperation with Nkrumah’s more ambitious and contentious Pan-African schemes.

events.name: Mali joins Ghana and Guinea in the Union of African States
events.summary: Quigley describes Mali joining Ghana and Guinea in July 1961 to form the Union of African States. He places this union in a competing set of African groupings, including the Casablanca connections and the more French-centered Brazzaville and Monrovia alignments.
details: Quigley describes Mali joining Ghana and Guinea in July 1961 to form the Union of African States. He places this union in a competing set of African groupings, including the Casablanca connections and the more French-centered Brazzaville and Monrovia alignments.

The author stresses rival national interests and divergent regional orientations rather than assuming that Pan-African rhetoric guaranteed durable integration. The union connects leaders’ ambitions, postcolonial aid needs and attempts to avoid fragmentation, while its limits illuminate the competition over who would define African cooperation.
events.context: The author stresses rival national interests and divergent regional orientations rather than assuming that Pan-African rhetoric guaranteed durable integration.

relationships.label: Commissioner and later chairman

relationships.label: Scientific adviser
relationships.description: Quigley places Oppenheimer among the committee’s scientists opposing a crash hydrogen-bomb program and advocating a more diversified defense response.

relationships.label: Advises nuclear policy
relationships.description: The GAC is the commission’s scientific advisory committee, distinct from the commissioners who ultimately make administrative decisions.

relationships.label: Advocates a second weapons laboratory
relationships.description: Quigley attributes the campaign for a second laboratory to Teller, supported by the Air Force after resistance from the AEC.

relationships.label: Strategic allies in thermonuclear advocacy
relationships.description: Quigley describes an alliance in defense-policy disputes, not a formal military membership: Teller’s H-bomb advocacy converged with Air Force preferences for strategic nuclear weapons.

relationships.label: Strategic-bombing command
relationships.description: Quigley discusses SAC wings, its bomber-centered role and its institutional opposition to nuclear diversification and defensive spending.

relationships.label: Weapons development institution
relationships.description: Quigley describes Los Alamos as part of the AEC weapons-development system, returning to increased activity through postwar nuclear programs.

relationships.label: Air-defense research funded through the Air Force
relationships.description: The Air Force helped initiate the laboratory’s research and controlled its budget, while Quigley describes resistance to expensive defensive recommendations.

relationships.label: Leads policy-planning work on NSC 68
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Nitze’s policy-planning staff as the sponsor of the strategic review that produced NSC 68.

relationships.label: Secretary of state
relationships.description: Acheson appears as secretary of state in the Pacific perimeter speech and concessions during the MacArthur hearings.

relationships.label: Selected as president
relationships.description: Quigley recounts the Columbia appointment after the Morgan-aligned succession impasse and Lamont’s death.

relationships.label: Long-serving president
relationships.description: Quigley describes Butler’s presidency and the prolonged difficulty of replacing him.

relationships.label: Academic spokesman in Quigley’s account
relationships.description: Quigley presents Butler as Morgan’s chief spokesman in university circles; this is the author’s interpretation of influence rather than a formal banking office.

relationships.label: Influence on presidential succession
relationships.description: Quigley describes Lamont and allies as able to preserve the status quo and block a successor without retaining the votes to choose a new president.

relationships.label: Corporate leader

relationships.label: Law-firm career before Senate appointment
relationships.description: Quigley describes Dulles’s longstanding Sullivan and Cromwell associations and his resignation from the firm in July 1949.

relationships.label: Earlier sponsorship in diplomatic work
relationships.description: Quigley describes Dulles’s 1945 introduction to Democratic foreign-policy work as occurring largely under Morgan sponsorship; this is not presented as employment by the bank.

relationships.label: Venue for massive-retaliation announcement
relationships.description: Quigley dates the public doctrine speech at the Council on Foreign Relations to January 12,1954. The connection records the venue, not an invented directorship.

relationships.label: Oil-cartel member

relationships.label: Effective leader of the officers’ conspiracy

relationships.label: Obtains declaration against Guatemala
